key_findings.finding: Passive ankle dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction reproduce the composite motion of pronation; therefore, pain with this maneuver most directly indicates a pronation-pattern ankle sprain rather than being specific for an isolated syndesmotic sprain. The maneuver tensions the medial ankle restraints, especially the deltoid ligament complex, and may also stress the interosseous/tibiofibular syndesmotic structures if external rotation or proximal syndesmotic tenderness is present.

source_tools.relevance: Directly defines pronation as the combination of eversion, dorsiflexion, and abduction.
Describes pronation–external-rotation injury as stressing the deltoid ligament and producing medial ankle injury.

key_findings.finding: Among the listed diagnoses, the best answer is a pronation ankle sprain with possible deltoid involvement—not a primary syndesmotic sprain based on this motion pattern alone. An isolated deltoid injury is usually associated with a forceful eversion/abduction (often external-rotation) mechanism and substantial force, whereas the described triad identifies the mechanism more broadly.

source_tools.relevance: Reports excessive abduction, eversion, and external rotation as mechanisms that injure the deltoid ligament, and notes that deltoid disruption requires considerable force.
Provides the direct pronation motion definition used to classify the examination pattern.

observations: Pain with passive dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction reproduces pronation and most directly indicates a pronation-pattern ankle sprain.
The mechanism may stress the medial ankle restraints, especially the deltoid ligament complex, and possibly the syndesmosis when external rotation or proximal syndesmotic tenderness is present.

source_tools.relevance: Supports the mechanism-based diagnosis from the clinical vignette.
Focused comparison of pronation, deltoid, and syndesmotic injuries.

entities.name: Syndesmotic ankle sprain
observations: An isolated syndesmotic sprain is more characteristically associated with external rotation and dorsiflexion, distal tibiofibular ligament pain, and positive squeeze or external-rotation tests.
The described pronation maneuver alone does not make syndesmotic sprain the primary diagnosis.

Supports interpretation of the provocative movement.

observations: A forceful eversion/abduction mechanism can injure the deltoid ligament, but the listed clinical motion pattern identifies a broader pronation mechanism rather than an isolated deltoid injury.
